title: Meet Jaspring
description: The reactive meta-framework for Java. Spring Boot foundations, Angular templates, and a different kind of full stack.

sections.title: A familiar, new stack
paragraphs: Jaspring connects Java, Spring, and Angular’s template language into one application model. Write components, services, pipes, and directives in Java. Describe the interface in HTML. Let signals and server-side change detection keep it live.

It is a meta-framework: Spring Boot provides the application foundation, dependency injection, and HTTP server; Angular’s real compiler parses the templates; Jaspring connects them with a component model, reactive state, and live HTML updates. The name brings those pieces together: Ja + Spri + ng.

sections.title: How a page lives
paragraphs: A Spring MVC controller returns a JaspringView. The server creates a component tree and renders the first HTML document, so content is available immediately. A small browser runtime then connects that page to the server.

When you click a bound button, the browser sends an event to the page. Its Java handler runs, signals change, and change detection collects the changed views. Jaspring sends HTML patches back over WebSocket, with HTTP as a fallback. Your application does not need a separate REST endpoint for each UI action.

sections.title: What you write
paragraphs: A component is a Java class with a Jaspring @Component annotation. Its template reads the class’s state and calls its methods. Services use ordinary Spring constructor injection.

sections.title: Growing in the open
paragraphs: Jaspring 0.5.0 is experimental and MIT licensed. The starter includes server rendering, live events, signals, change detection, and the browser APIs: client hooks, browser calls, and Java browser closures compiled to WebAssembly. Browser scripts can be written in TypeScript. Static generation and incremental regeneration are future work.
Start with a small application, try the live examples, and review the compatibility guide before adopting Angular-specific assumptions. Installation targets Jaspring 0.5.0.

JNPM is included in Jaspring 0.5.0. Declare browser npm dependencies in Gradle and build them with package typings, bundling and ESLint. The JNPM, Chart.js and Font Awesome guides use the release artifacts from Maven Central.
sections.note: This website is itself a Jaspring application. Its live counter, search results, and navigation state run as Java components, and its one browser script is written in TypeScript.

title: Installation
description: Start from the ready-made starter project, or add Jaspring to an existing Gradle or Maven application.

sections.title: Before you begin
paragraphs: Use Java 25 and Spring Boot 4.1.x. Oracle GraalVM 25.2.4 matches the bundled GraalJS runtime and enables optimized startup compilation. Other Java 25 distributions work with the interpreter and can start more slowly.

Use Gradle for the supported TypeScript build and JNPM workflow. Apply the Jaspring plugin alongside the Spring Boot starter: the plugin provides build tooling, while the starter provides the application runtime. Keep their Jaspring versions aligned.

You do not need to install Node.js, npm or Angular CLI yourself. The Angular, styling and TypeScript compilers are bundled; JNPM manages Node/npm automatically at build time when npm packages are declared. Java browser closures are optional and have extra requirements, covered in WebAssembly build.

sections.title: Start from the starter project
paragraphs: The fastest way to begin is the starter project. It is a complete Gradle application with the plugin, the Spring Boot starter, a live counter page, a test and the Gradle wrapper already set up. It uses Jaspring 0.5.0.
Download and unzip it, then run it. Open http://localhost:8080/ and click the button. Rename the com.example package to your own when you are ready.
To add Jaspring to an existing Spring Boot application instead, follow the sections below. They set up the same files by hand.
sections.code:
unzip jaspring-starter.zip
cd jaspring-starter
./gradlew bootRun

sections.title: Resolve the Gradle plugin
paragraphs: The Jaspring Gradle plugin and its marker are published to Maven Central. Add Maven Central to pluginManagement.repositories in settings.gradle; the repositories block in build.gradle only resolves library dependencies.
Keep pluginManagement as the first block in settings.gradle. If it already exists, merge these repositories into it.

sections.title: Apply the plugin and add the starter
paragraphs: Add the Jaspring plugin to your existing Spring Boot plugins block, keeping the java plugin applied. The plugin type-checks and compiles src/main/typescript during the build and packages the browser scripts with the application. It also provides component generation and the optional WebAssembly build.

Add the starter for the runtime and Spring Boot’s WebSocket starter for the default live transport; without WebSocket support, Jaspring uses HTTP. The optional developmentOnly compiler dependency enables the package-free TypeScript startup fallback for IDE launches that bypass Gradle.

The bootRun JVM arguments let the bundled GraalJS runtime use native access, and stop Java 25 from printing a sun.misc.Unsafe warning at startup. Add them to the test task too when your tests start the application.
JNPM is included in the 0.5.0 Gradle plugin below. Follow the JNPM guide to declare browser packages, generate jnpm.lock and bundle the application.

sections.title: Using Maven with limitations
paragraphs: The Spring Boot starter works in a Maven application, but Maven cannot apply the Jaspring Gradle plugin. There is no equivalent Jaspring Maven build plugin. Review the limitations before choosing Maven for an application that needs TypeScript, JNPM or Java browser closures.

Use these starter dependencies in an existing Spring Boot Maven project. Configure --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED and --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow for the Java process that starts the application.
sections.code:
<dependency>
    <groupId>dev.isira</groupId>
    <artifactId>jaspring-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>0.5.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-websocket</artifactId>
</dependency>

sections.title: Create a component
paragraphs: Place the component under your @SpringBootApplication package so Jaspring can discover it. Here the package is com.example.components. These imports belong to Jaspring, including @Component.

sections.title: Give it a template
paragraphs: Resources follow the component’s package. A relative templateUrl is resolved next to the class on the classpath.
sections.code:
Hello, Jaspring.

Count: {{ count() }}

sections.title: Return it from a controller
paragraphs: JaspringView is a Spring MVC view. Return one from a controller, then start your app with ./gradlew bootRun and visit http://localhost:8080/.
sections.note: The starter supplies a default layout. To customize the document head, add src/main/resources/jaspring/index.html containing <app-counter></app-counter>.

title: Components
description: Java classes with an interface. Compose them into a tree, pass inputs, and let Spring provide the dependencies.

sections.title: Define a component
paragraphs: Use dev.isira.jaspring.component.Component to register a selector, template, and optional stylesheet. Jaspring creates component instances per live page through Spring’s bean factory. They are not shared singleton UI objects.

sections.title: Inputs and composition
paragraphs: A parent uses a child’s selector as an HTML element. Bind a property to pass an input. Components, pipes, and directives discovered by the application are currently available globally; Angular’s standalone imports lists are not enforced.
sections.code: Hello, {{ name }}.

sections.title: Send values to the parent
paragraphs: Create an OutputEmitter with Signals.output() and annotate it with @Output. Emitting a value invokes the parent’s bound handler during the current page turn.

sections.title: Work with the lifecycle
paragraphs: Implement lifecycle interfaces from dev.isira.jaspring.cd.lifecycle, such as OnInit, OnChanges, AfterViewInit, and OnDestroy. Their methods use familiar names like ngOnInit() and ngOnDestroy().

Use initialization to load component data and destruction to release owned resources. Constructor injection works for services. When work should complete after the first response, use the page’s Zone.fork API so the continuation runs inside a valid turn.
sections.note: Sibling hook phases are not batched exactly like Angular. Each child runs its pre-render hooks and renders before the next sibling. Within a component, the hook order follows Angular.

title: Templates
description: Angular’s template language, interpreted against your Java components. The real compiler handles the syntax.

sections.title: Read state and handle events
paragraphs: Interpolation escapes text. Property bindings reflect values into the corresponding HTML attributes. Event bindings call Java methods or update signals. Read a signal with count() in the template, corresponding to count.get() in Java.
sections.code:
{{ title }}

Hello, {{ name() }}

{{ count() }}

sections.title: Use native control flow
paragraphs: Use @if, @for, and @switch directly. Track list items by a stable key to preserve child component instances. Loops expose $index, $first, $last, $even, $odd, and $count.

sections.title: Transform and reuse
paragraphs: Built-in pipes include case transforms, date, number, percent, currency, json, keyvalue, slice, and async. Custom Java pipes implement PipeTransform and use Jaspring’s @Pipe annotation.
Structural forms such as *ngIf, *ngFor, ngSwitch, and ngTemplateOutlet are supported too. Use ng-content for projection, and ng-template for a reusable template fragment.
sections.code:
{{ title | uppercase }}

{{ user | json }}

{{ total | currency:'USD' }}

sections.title: Understand the boundaries
paragraphs: Expressions follow JavaScript semantics: strict and loose equality are distinct; optional chaining short-circuits; integral arithmetic results normalize to integers. Java methods and typed signals receive coerced argument values.

Text is escaped. URL bindings use Angular-derived security contexts. innerHTML is sanitized unless given an explicitly trusted SafeHtml. Template references on ordinary elements are server-side ElementRef values, not live browser DOM nodes.
sections.note: @defer currently renders a placeholder, or the main content for hydrate triggers. Server-side triggers do not fire. See Compatibility for the full behavioral differences.

title: Signals & state
description: Small primitives. Connected state. A reactive graph that follows the values your interface actually reads.

sections.title: Start with a value
paragraphs: Signals.signal(initialValue) returns a WritableSignal<T>. Read it with get(), replace it with set(), or derive its next value with update(). Templates read a signal using function-call syntax.

sections.title: Let derived state follow
paragraphs: Signals.computed(supplier) produces a read-only Signal<T>. It tracks the signals read during the calculation and recomputes lazily when needed. Dependencies are rebuilt on each run, so conditional reads naturally change what it observes.

sections.title: Effects and linked state
paragraphs: Signals.effect runs side effects through a scheduler. Effects created in component constructors or lifecycle hooks belong to the page and run before views during the next tick. A cleanup registrar can release resources between runs or at destruction.

Signals.linkedSignal derives a writable value from another signal. Signals.untracked reads without adding dependencies. Input, model, and output primitives are available through Signals.input(), inputRequired(), model(), and output().

sections.title: Respect page ownership
paragraphs: Signals created in a page turn remember that page. Write them from event handlers, lifecycle work, or Zone-managed continuations. A write from an unrelated thread throws SignalWriteOutsideTurnException.

Default equality is Java’s Objects.equals, which works naturally with records and value collections. Angular uses identity equality. Pass Equality.identity() when that behavior is needed. Do not write signals from a computed calculation.
sections.note: Signals created in singleton services outside a page turn are shared and unguarded. Keep visitor-specific state in components or page-scoped services.

title: Events & forms
description: A browser interaction becomes a Java turn. Bind directly to methods and keep form values in sync.

sections.title: Bind an event
paragraphs: Use Angular’s event binding syntax. The browser serializes the event, the server evaluates its expression, and change detection sends back any changed views. The $event value exposes serialized fields such as target.value and custom-event detail.
sections.code:
<button (click)="save()">Save</button>
<input (keyup.enter)="search($event.target.value)">
<canvas data-jsp-hook="chart"
        (point-picked)="select($event.detail.index)"></canvas>

sections.title: Keep a form in sync
paragraphs: Two-way ngModel works with plain writable fields and WritableSignal values. Use a submit handler for form actions; the browser runtime prevents the default submit navigation. Validate external values in Java before using them.
sections.code:
<form (submit)="save()">
  <label for="name">Your name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" [(ngModel)]="name" required>
  <button type="submit" [disabled]="saving()">Save</button>
</form>

sections.title: Control browser defaults
paragraphs: The server cannot cancel a browser action after the network trip. Jaspring decides preventDefault and stopPropagation from the handler when it renders.

An expression ending in false or calling $event.preventDefault() gets a prevent-default flag. Calling $event.stopPropagation() adds a stop-propagation flag. The browser applies those flags before sending the event.
sections.code: Open panel

sections.title: Choose the transport
paragraphs: WebSocket is the default and uses one connection per page. If it cannot connect, the runtime falls back to HTTP. HTTP posts events and polls while asynchronous work is pending. Transport off renders ordinary HTML without live handlers or the client runtime.
sections.code:
jaspring:
  live:
    transport: websocket # websocket, http, or off

title: Services & injection
description: Keep your existing Spring habits. Inject services into components and give page state the right lifetime.

sections.title: Use ordinary Spring services
paragraphs: Jaspring creates components through Spring’s bean factory, so constructor injection works without another container. Keep business rules and external I/O behind services, then pass the results into component state.

sections.title: Give state a page lifetime
paragraphs: Spring services are singletons by default. A mutable singleton is shared across visitors. Use @Scope("jaspring-page") for a bean that should be owned by one live page. The scope is available during rendering, event handlers, and tracked continuations.

sections.title: Return to a page turn
paragraphs: Zone.current().fork(work) performs work outside the page turn on a virtual thread. Its continuation runs as a new turn, under the page lock. That is the safe place to update the component’s page-owned signals.
sections.note: Use a short jaspring.stability-timeout when you want the initial HTML to respond before slow work finishes. The result then arrives as a patch.

title: Styles & Tailwind
description: Scoped component CSS or Tailwind v4. Both are processed on the JVM when your application starts.

sections.title: Keep styles close
paragraphs: Set styleUrl on @Component to load CSS relative to the component’s classpath package. Inline styles are also supported. PostCSS transforms component styles once at startup.

sections.title: Emulated encapsulation
paragraphs: Jaspring adds scope attributes to component elements and rewrites selectors, matching Angular’s emulated style encapsulation. :host targets the component host. :host-context handles ancestor context. Selectors after ::ng-deep remain unscoped.
The layout emits processed component styles in a head style block. Put global resets, font declarations, and site-wide tokens in a static stylesheet linked from your layout.

sections.title: Enable Tailwind v4
paragraphs: Point jaspring.tailwind.stylesheet at a classpath stylesheet. Tailwind v4 runs in GraalJS at startup, using class candidates found in compiled templates and the layout. No Node-based file scanner is needed.

sections.title: Use utilities deliberately
paragraphs: Component styles can use @apply and theme variables. Jaspring compiles them with a reference to your Tailwind stylesheet before scoping them.
Keep utility class names complete and visible in templates so the candidate scanner can find them. Tailwind @plugin and @config are unavailable because no Node code executes in this pipeline.

title: Browser interop
description: Jaspring renders on the server. When work belongs in the browser, reach it with JavaScript hooks and calls, or with Java closures compiled to WebAssembly.

sections.title: Two ways to reach the browser
paragraphs: Some work only the browser can do: draw on a canvas, read localStorage, ask for the user's location, or wrap a JavaScript widget. Jaspring gives you two tools for it. Both use the same page connection as events and patches.

Client hooks and browser calls are JavaScript, written in TypeScript under src/main/typescript or as plain scripts. Use them for widgets, third-party libraries, and pages where every kilobyte counts. Java browser closures are Java lambdas compiled to WebAssembly at build time. Use them when you want one language and can afford the runtime download.
sections.code:
Client hooks        JavaScript bound to an element's lifetime
                    data-jsp-hook + jaspring.hooks.register
Browser calls       Java asks the browser for a value
                    Browser.current().call(...) + jaspring.calls.register
Browser closures    A Java lambda runs in the browser as WebAssembly
                    Platform.onBrowser(client -> ...)

sections.title: Choose the right tool
paragraphs: Use a client hook when an element needs browser code for its whole life: a chart, a map, a canvas, or a date picker. Use a browser call when Java needs one answer from the browser, such as a size, a stored value, or the result of a widget method. Use a Java closure when you want to write that browser code in Java and the WebAssembly build fits your toolchain.

Hooks and calls work with any Java 25 runtime. In TypeScript they need only the Jaspring Gradle plugin, which bundles the compiler. Java closures need Oracle GraalVM with Web Image and Binaryen at build time, and a browser with WebAssembly GC support at run time.

sections.title: How a browser round trip works
paragraphs: Browser work is part of the page protocol. A call sent during an event travels with that turn's patches, after them, so a hook mounted by a patch exists before a call targets it. A call made while the page is first rendered travels with the document and does not delay it.
The answer returns to the same page. Jaspring completes the ZoneTask inside a page turn, so the continuation may write signals. Changed views go out as patches, exactly like the result of a fork.
sections.code:
Java handler → Browser.current().call("viewport")
    → call message (after this turn's patches)
    → registered JavaScript function runs
    → result message
    → ZoneTask completes inside a page turn
    → signal writes → patches

sections.title: Know the boundaries
paragraphs: The server owns the markup. When a view changes, the browser runtime morphs its host element to the new server HTML. DOM changes made by browser code inside that view are transient, so keep lasting state in signals, and keep widget state in the hook or closure, not in the markup.

Everything sent to the browser is visible to the user. Never pass secrets as call arguments, hook parameters, or closure captures. Treat values coming back from the browser as user input and validate them in Java.

With jaspring.live.transport=off there is no client runtime and no compiled TypeScript scripts are added to the page. Every browser call and closure fails at once with BrowserCallException, and hand-linked page scripts must not expect window.jaspring.

title: Client hooks
description: Bind JavaScript to an element's lifetime. Hooks mount, update, and clean up as patches change the page.

sections.title: Mark the element
paragraphs: Add data-jsp-hook with the hook name to any element in a template. Pass data with data-jsp-hook-params. The value is parsed as JSON, so the json pipe is the easy way to send a list, a map, or a record.
Nothing on the server knows about hooks. The template only has an attribute and, if needed, an ordinary event binding.
sections.code:
<canvas width="240" height="60"
        data-jsp-hook="sparkline"
        [attr.data-jsp-hook-params]="points() | json"
        (point-picked)="pick($event.detail.index)"></canvas>

sections.title: Register the hook
paragraphs: Register the hook from a page script with jaspring.hooks.register(name, hook). Page scripts are TypeScript files under src/main/typescript. Each method receives the element and a context object. Register at any time: elements already on the page mount as soon as their hook is registered.
The type parameters name the element type and the params type, so el is an HTMLCanvasElement and ctx.params is a number[] here. The jaspring global is typed by the compiler's bundled jaspring.d.ts.

sections.title: Follow the lifecycle
paragraphs: mounted runs when a hooked element is in the document: at page load, after a patch adds it, or when the hook is registered later. updated runs after a patch morphs the view that contains the element; ctx.params is read again first. destroyed runs when the element leaves the document.
A hook can define more methods. They do not run on their own. The server calls them with Browser.current().call("hook.method"), as described in Browser calls.
Errors thrown by mounted, updated, or destroyed are logged to the browser console and do not stop the page.
sections.code:
mounted(el, ctx)     element entered the document
updated(el, ctx)     its view was patched; ctx.params is fresh
destroyed(el, ctx)   element left the document
other(el, ctx, ...)  called by the server as "hook.other"

sections.title: Use the context
paragraphs: ctx.el is the element. ctx.name is the hook name. ctx.page is the live page id. ctx.params is the parsed data-jsp-hook-params value: an empty object when the attribute is missing, and the raw string when it is not valid JSON.
ctx.pushEvent(type, detail) dispatches a bubbling CustomEvent from the element. The component receives it through an ordinary binding such as (point-picked)="pick($event.detail.index)".

sections.title: One hook object, many elements
paragraphs: A registered hook is one object shared by every element that uses its name. this points to that shared object, so keep helpers as module functions and do not store per-element state on the hook.
Keep per-element state in a WeakMap keyed by the element. The entry goes away with the element.

sections.title: Patches and hook-managed DOM
paragraphs: A patch morphs the whole view to the server's HTML, including the hooked element and its children. Attributes, inline styles, and child nodes that your script added are removed when the enclosing view changes. Then updated runs. Canvas pixels are not DOM and survive a morph.

Add data-jsp-ignore to an element whose DOM a widget owns, such as an editor, a map, a date picker, or a Chart.js canvas. A patch then keeps its children and attributes, and only adds or updates its data-* attributes, so new data-jsp-hook-params still reach updated. Give the element a stable id so the morph always matches it to the same node. Remove data-jsp-ignore from the template and the next patch morphs the element again.

sections.title: Scripts reach the page by themselves
paragraphs: Every top-level file in src/main/typescript gets a <script type="module"> tag after the client runtime, so you do not edit the layout. Module scripts are deferred, so window.jaspring exists when they run, wherever they stand in the document.
Plain JavaScript still works. Put it under src/main/resources/static and link it from the layout, src/main/resources/jaspring/index.html, with type="module" or defer.

JNPM also bundles imported npm packages and their assets. Its entrypoints still load after the runtime, so the hook lifecycle stays the same. See JNPM and Third-party JavaScript for the package setup.
sections.code:
<body>
  <app-root>…</app-root>
  <script src="/_jaspring/idiomorph.min.js"></script>
  <script src="/_jaspring/jaspring.js" data-jsp-page="…" data-jsp-transport="websocket"></script>
  <script type="module" src="/_jaspring/ts/sparkline.js?v=574f4503"></script>
</body>
sections.note: With jaspring.live.transport=off the runtime is not loaded and compiled scripts are not added. Guard hand-linked shared scripts with if (window.jaspring) when a page may render without it.

title: Browser calls
description: Ask the browser for a value from Java. The answer comes back inside a page turn, ready to write signals.

sections.title: Register a page function
paragraphs: Register a function with jaspring.calls.register(name, fn) from a page script under src/main/typescript. The function receives the call arguments and returns a JSON value or a promise of one.

sections.title: Call it from Java
paragraphs: Get the browser with Browser.current() inside a turn: a constructor, a lifecycle hook, an event handler, or a fork continuation. call(target, args...) returns a ZoneTask. Its continuation runs inside a page turn, so it may write signals.
Arguments are sent as JSON. Use strings, numbers, booleans, lists, maps, and records of those.

sections.title: Call a hook method
paragraphs: A dotted target such as sparkline.size runs the size method of the sparkline hook mounted inside the current component's host element. The method receives (el, ctx, ...args).
Obtain Browser.current() in the component that owns the hooked element. A dotted target with no current component fails at once with IllegalStateException.
sections.code:
Browser.current().call("sparkline.size")
        .thenAccept(size -> status.set("canvas " + size));

sections.title: Read the result
paragraphs: The value arrives as parsed JSON: Map, List, String, Number, Boolean, or null. undefined becomes null. The type parameter of call is an unchecked cast, so read numbers as Number and convert them.

Over the WebSocket a result may be up to 4 MiB characters. The server joins message fragments itself, so the servlet container's text buffer, 8 KB on Tomcat, does not apply. Send images, files, and large documents to an ordinary endpoint instead.

sections.title: Handle failures
paragraphs: The task fails with BrowserCallException when the browser function throws or rejects, when the target is not registered, when the result is larger than the WebSocket limit, when no answer arrives within 30 seconds, or when live events are off. An oversized result fails at once, not after the timeout. Destroying the page cancels open calls.
whenComplete usually receives a CompletionException. The browser's reason is its cause.
The page stays unstable until the answer arrives. Over HTTP, the client keeps polling until every open call is answered.

title: TypeScript
description: Write hooks and page functions in TypeScript. The Gradle plugin checks the sources and the page loads them automatically; JNPM adds npm packages and bundling.

sections.title: Typed browser scripts
paragraphs: Client hooks, page functions for browser calls, and any other code that runs in the page can be written in TypeScript. Put the files in src/main/typescript. The Gradle plugin type-checks and compiles them before the application runs, and Jaspring adds them to every live page.
Nothing in production runs the compiler. The jar holds plain JavaScript, served as ES modules under /_jaspring/ts/.
sections.code:
src/main/typescript/
  sparkline.ts      entry point  → /_jaspring/ts/sparkline.js
  app.ts            entry point  → /_jaspring/ts/app.js
  lib/bars.ts       module, reached through imports
  chart.d.ts        global types, emits nothing
sections.note: The unbundled URLs below describe package-free applications. JNPM emits hashed entrypoints and shared chunks; see the JNPM guide.

sections.title: Set up the build
paragraphs: Apply the Jaspring Gradle plugin with the same version as the starter. It bundles TypeScript 6.0.3 and runs it in GraalJS inside a Gradle worker, so there is nothing to install.

The developmentOnly dependency is optional. In a package-free application it enables the source-only startup fallback described below. JNPM applications build before launch; their development compiler detects stale bundles instead of rebuilding packages at startup. The dependency is not part of the packaged application.

sections.title: Entry points and modules
paragraphs: Top-level .ts files are entrypoints and get script tags in the page. Files in subdirectories are supporting modules. Without JNPM, each file is emitted separately and nested paths are kept; import siblings with a .js extension, or a .ts extension that the compiler rewrites. With JNPM, entrypoints and imported packages are bundled, and shared modules become shared chunks.

The jaspring global is typed everywhere. Its types are also importable from "jaspring": Hook, HookContext, CallFn, and Global. The typings come from the client runtime's own source, so they match what runs.

sections.title: Fixed compiler options
paragraphs: The compiler options are fixed. The import rule, the served format, and the editor setup depend on them. strict mode is on.
sections.code:
target                 es2022
module                 esnext
moduleResolution       bundler
lib                    es2022, dom
strict                 true
isolatedModules        true
verbatimModuleSyntax   true
every file             a module

sections.title: The build tasks
paragraphs: For package-free applications, extractTypescriptTypes and compileTypescript run before processResources. Projects without TypeScript sources skip compilation. JNPM also installs the lock and prepares package declarations before compilation, then bundles the checked sources; check includes ESLint.

A GraalVM JDK makes the compiler several times faster. The plugin uses GRAALVM_HOME, or the JDK running Gradle when it is GraalVM. On GraalVM 25, loading the compiler takes about 3 seconds and a type-checked compile of a few files about 6 seconds; a warm compile takes under 1 second. Gradle's worker daemons keep it warm between builds, and the task is cached like any other.
sections.code:
extractTypescriptTypes   jaspring.d.ts and tsconfig.base.json
                         → build/jaspring/typescript/types/
compileTypescript        type-check and compile src/main/typescript
                         → jaspring/ts/**/*.js and jaspring/jaspring-typescript.json
                           in the application's resources

sections.title: Configure the build
paragraphs: The typescript block is optional; these are the defaults. host = NODE runs the same bundled compiler in a Node 20 or later process, which starts and compiles faster. The output is identical, so the host is a developer's choice, not a project setting.

Each setting has a Gradle property for one-off builds: -Pjaspring.typescript.typeCheck=false transpiles without checking, -Pjaspring.typescript.host=node picks Node, -Pjaspring.typescript.nodePath points to a Node binary, and -Pjaspring.typescript.skip=true skips the build. By default the first Node 20+ on the PATH is used.

sections.title: Type errors fail the build
paragraphs: Type errors fail compileTypescript in tsc's format. Paths are relative to the project root, so IDE consoles make them clickable.
sections.code:
> Task :compileTypescript FAILED
src/main/typescript/sparkline.ts(12,5): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

sections.title: Set up the editor
paragraphs: Add a tsconfig.json to the project root. IntelliJ IDEA and VS Code then check the sources with the build's options and the jaspring typings. Run any build, or ./gradlew extractTypescriptTypes, once so the extended file exists.

JNPM applications extend build/jaspring/typescript/types/tsconfig.jnpm.json instead. Run prepareJnpmTypes first to expose the installed package declarations. Its IntelliJ integration also supplies ESLint diagnostics for unsaved text.

sections.title: How scripts reach the page
paragraphs: /_jaspring/ts/** serves the compiled files with a one-hour cache, or no-cache in dev mode. The layout gets one tag per entry point after the client runtime. The source digest is in the URL, so browsers fetch a new build at once.

Module scripts are deferred, so they run after the classic jaspring.js tag and jaspring is always defined. The tags are added only together with the runtime: with jaspring.live.transport=off there is no runtime and no page scripts. Scripts linked by hand in the layout keep working; they must be type="module" or placed after the runtime.
JNPM changes entry filenames to include content hashes and also serves shared chunks, CSS and referenced assets. Bundle styles are linked once in the head; only entry modules receive script tags.
sections.code:
<script src="/_jaspring/jaspring.js" data-jsp-page="…" data-jsp-transport="websocket"></script>
<script type="module" src="/_jaspring/ts/sparkline.js?v=574f4503"></script>

sections.title: Startup fallback
paragraphs: For applications without JNPM, the build's manifest records a digest per source file. With dev.isira:jaspring-typescript on the runtime classpath, the starter compares it at startup with src/main/typescript next to the working directory, or with classpath:/typescript/ when that directory is absent. It compiles when the manifest is missing or stale: an IDE run that bypassed Gradle, or a build without the plugin. The result is served from memory.
Compile errors fail startup, like a template that Angular rejects. A packaged application has no sources, so its manifest stands and nothing runs. In Maven, use the runtime scope for the dependency.
sections.code:
jaspring:
  typescript:
    enabled: true            # the fallback at all
    type-check: true         # false transpiles without checking
    source-dir: src/main/typescript
    host: graaljs            # or node
sections.note: JNPM requires a frontend build before launch. Its development startup checks reject stale or missing bundles and never run npm or esbuild. Run ./gradlew compileTypescript, or use bootRun or the IntelliJ before-run task.

sections.title: Limits
paragraphs: Spring devtools does not watch .ts files. Run ./gradlew compileTypescript after editing them. Package-free applications can also use their startup fallback; JNPM applications must rebuild before restarting.

Without JNPM, scripts import sibling modules and external scripts need local declarations. JNPM adds npm imports, package typings and bundling. Node/OS APIs remain unsupported in browser code; imports such as fs fail the JNPM build, including transitive imports.

TypeScript 6 is the last JavaScript release of the compiler; 7.x is a native binary. Language features after the 6.x line would need a native host. A JVM without GraalVM's optimizing compiler runs the compiler interpreted, about twice as slow on a cold start, and the build says so. host = NODE avoids that where Node is installed.
sections.note: This website's own browser script is src/main/typescript/site.ts. It handles syntax coloring, clipboard access, keyboard shortcuts, and dialog focus.

title: JNPM
description: Declare npm browser packages in Gradle, lock their versions, and bundle JavaScript, CSS and assets during the build. Included in Jaspring 0.5.0.

sections.title: Browser packages, declared in Gradle
paragraphs: JNPM means Java npm. Add a top-level jnpm block to build.gradle or build.gradle.kts. Java owns the Gradle workflow, npm resolves the packages, and esbuild bundles them for the browser. No project package.json or separate npm install command is needed.
The generated package.json, package-lock.json and node_modules all live under build/. Each application module owns its jnpm.lock beside build.gradle. Commit that lock with the declarations.
sections.note: This guide requires the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin and matching starter. Follow Installation for the Maven Central setup.

sections.title: Use Jaspring 0.5.0
paragraphs: JNPM is included in the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin. Resolve the plugin and libraries from Maven Central and keep the plugin, starter and any explicit jaspring-typescript dependency on the same version.
The application needs Java 25. JNPM downloads its checksum-pinned Node/npm toolchain at build time. Node and npm are not required on the production server.

sections.title: Use matching Gradle dependencies
paragraphs: Add Maven Central to both plugin repositories and library repositories, then apply the matching Jaspring release. This example uses Groovy; the jnpm dependency methods also work in Kotlin DSL.

sections.title: Choose the dependency scope
paragraphs: implementation supplies browser runtime JavaScript and any typings included by the package. api supplies additional declarations, such as @types packages. It does not export dependencies to other Gradle projects as Java’s api configuration does.

devImplementation supplies development tools, and devApi supplies their declarations. These development scopes are excluded from application imports and browser bundles. Node-based tools can run during the build; application packages must work in the browser.

Use package:version or package:semver-range, including scoped package names. Declare a package in one scope only. Runtime imports require a direct implementation declaration; type-only imports may also use api. An undeclared transitive package is not an application import.
sections.code:
jnpm {
    implementation("nanoid:5.1.6")
    implementation("lodash-es:^4.17.21")
    api("@types/lodash-es:^4.17.12")
    devImplementation("prettier:3.6.2")
    devApi("@types/node:^22")
}

sections.title: Lock, install and build
paragraphs: Run jnpmLock after adding or changing declarations, then commit jnpm.lock. It reconciles the declarations while retaining compatible locked versions. jnpmUpdate explicitly refreshes packages within the declared ranges.

Normal builds install the exact lock with npm ci. A missing or mismatched lock fails with instructions to run jnpmLock; a normal build never rewrites the committed lock. Use qualified tasks such as :app:jnpmLock in a multi-project build.

clean removes build/node_modules and generated metadata. The managed toolchain and npm download cache survive under Gradle’s user cache. After the dependencies have been cached, --offline can reinstall them following clean. A cache miss fails instead of downloading.
sections.code:
./gradlew jnpmLock
# Commit build.gradle and jnpm.lock.
./gradlew build

# Later, deliberately refresh versions within the ranges:
./gradlew jnpmUpdate

# After an online build has populated the cache:
./gradlew clean build --offline

sections.title: The JNPM tasks
paragraphs: compileTypescript prepares the installation and declarations before checking and bundling. check and build also run lintTypescript. fixTypescript is an explicit source-changing operation; normal linting only reports diagnostics.
sections.code:
jnpmLock           create or reconcile jnpm.lock
jnpmUpdate         refresh locked versions within the ranges
jnpmInstall        install the exact lock into build/node_modules
prepareJnpmTypes   prepare declarations, editor config and IDE metadata
compileTypescript  type-check and bundle browser entrypoints
lintTypescript     report ESLint diagnostics; included in check
fixTypescript      apply ESLint fixes to source files

sections.title: Import a package from TypeScript
paragraphs: Keep entrypoints directly under src/main/typescript and supporting modules in subdirectories. Import npm packages by name. Typings shipped by implementation packages are discovered automatically; add an api dependency when a package needs separate declarations.

Public exports, supported subpaths and browser entrypoints are resolved from the installed packages. ESM and CommonJS dependencies are supported. The compiler checks the TypeScript, then esbuild emits minified ES2022 modules and shared chunks with hashed names.
sections.code:
import { nanoid } from "nanoid";

jaspring.calls.register("newId", () => nanoid());

sections.title: Browser APIs only
paragraphs: Application packages run in the browser. Imports of fs, node:fs, path, net, child_process and other Node/OS APIs fail the build, including imports inside dependencies. JNPM does not add Node polyfills.

A package with separate browser and Node entrypoints can work when its selected browser implementation avoids those APIs. Installing a package successfully does not establish browser compatibility; the bundle must also build.

ESLint and other development tools run in the managed Node process during the build and never enter the application bundle. Dependency lifecycle scripts are disabled. Packages that need postinstall compilation or native Node addons are unsupported.

sections.title: Ship CSS, fonts and other assets
paragraphs: Import CSS and static assets from a browser entrypoint. JNPM emits CSS, referenced fonts and images, JSON imports and literal dynamic imports with the browser build. CSS url() references are rewritten to emitted asset paths.

Jaspring loads bundle styles once in the page head and adds entry modules after its client runtime. Bundle CSS loads eagerly. JavaScript chunks, source maps, assets, license notices and the manifest are packaged in the JAR; node_modules and the build tools are not.

Failed type checking or bundling leaves the previous successful bundle in place. A successful rebuild removes obsolete chunks. The Font Awesome cookbook shows a package stylesheet and its fonts going through this pipeline.

sections.title: Set up TypeScript completion
paragraphs: Run prepareJnpmTypes, then extend tsconfig.jnpm.json from the project’s tsconfig.json. The generated configuration maps public package imports to installed declarations and includes the jaspring typings.

A separate tool or test tsconfig can extend tsconfig.jnpm.dev.json to include development scopes. Browser sources do not automatically receive Node globals. Avoid blanket paths aliases into build/node_modules; the generated declaration mappings are for the editor.

sections.title: Lint the browser sources
paragraphs: ESLint is enabled by default, using the recommended JavaScript and TypeScript ESLint rules with browser globals and jaspring. Errors fail check; warnings are reported. The JSON report is written to build/reports/jnpm/eslint.json.

An optional eslint.config.mjs at the application root replaces the defaults. Its imports resolve against build/node_modules. Declare additional compatible ESLint plugins in devImplementation. JNPM pins ESLint, its standard config, TypeScript ESLint, TypeScript, esbuild and globals; conflicting overrides are rejected.
To disable linting, use jnpm { lint { enabled.set(false) } } and reconcile the lock after changing the generated tool dependencies.

sections.title: Use the IntelliJ integration
paragraphs: Build the Jaspring IntelliJ plugin from the same framework checkout. With Gradle support enabled, sync imports the JNPM model, registers package roots as libraries and runs prepareJnpmTypes. Application run configurations receive a compileTypescript before-run task.
With JavaScript/TypeScript support installed, the plugin runs managed ESLint against unsaved editor text and offers diagnostics and fixes. It uses the same ESLint configuration as the Gradle task.

Tools → JNPM provides Prepare Dependencies, Reconcile Dependency Lock and Update Dependencies. Reconcile a missing lock explicitly; sync does not create it. After clean, prepare dependencies again. Template features still work without the optional Gradle and JavaScript integrations.

sections.title: Build before starting the application
paragraphs: JNPM packages are never installed or bundled at application startup. bootRun and the IntelliJ integration build the frontend before launching. Other launch paths must run compileTypescript first.

With jaspring-typescript present for development, missing or stale JNPM bundles produce an instruction to build. Startup checks the sources, referenced assets and lockfile against the manifest. Package-free applications keep the existing source-only startup compiler.

sections.title: Use a private registry
paragraphs: Configure registries in Gradle. A scoped registry serves its listed scopes; a registry without scopes replaces npmjs.org. Names use letters, digits and underscores, and scopes must be unique.

URLs use HTTPS, except for loopback test registries. Supply bearer tokens through Gradle providers, normally from environment variables. Generated npm configuration contains environment-variable references, not token values. User and global npm configuration are not inherited.

sections.title: Toolchain and current limits
paragraphs: The managed default is a checksum-pinned Node 22.23.1 distribution. Linux, macOS and Windows on x64 and ARM64 have configured distributions. To use a centrally managed distribution, set jnpm.nodeHome or -Pjnpm.nodeHome=/path/to/node. It must contain npm and Node 22.15+ on the 22.x line, or Node 24+.

The first implementation accepts registry packages with exact versions or semver ranges. Dist-tags, Git, file, URL and workspace dependencies are unsupported. JSX setup, HMR, npm publishing and JavaScript test execution remain separate work.

title: Third-party JavaScript
description: Install a browser library through JNPM and wrap it in a typed client hook. This guide uses Chart.js with bundled declarations.

sections.title: The pattern
paragraphs: Declare the library in jnpm, lock it and import it from TypeScript. Jaspring bundles the library with the hook and adds the entry script automatically. Package typings are discovered during the build.

This page builds a Chart.js bar chart. Keep widget state in a client hook, preserve its element with data-jsp-ignore, pass data through hook parameters, and send user actions to Java with ctx.pushEvent.
sections.code:
1. Declare the library   jnpm { implementation("chart.js:4.6.1") }
2. Lock the dependency   ./gradlew jnpmLock; commit jnpm.lock
3. Import and wrap it    src/main/typescript/chart-hook.ts
4. Build it              ./gradlew build
5. Feed it               [attr.data-jsp-hook-params]="data | json"
6. Listen                ctx.pushEvent → (event)="handler()"
7. Ask it                Browser.current().call("chart.total")
sections.note: This guide requires the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin and matching starter. Follow Installation for the Maven Central setup.

sections.title: Add the library
paragraphs: Add Chart.js as a browser implementation dependency. Its npm package includes TypeScript declarations, so this example needs no api dependency. JNPM installs the package under build/node_modules.
Run ./gradlew jnpmLock after adding the declaration and commit jnpm.lock. Later builds use that exact graph. Use ./gradlew jnpmUpdate when you deliberately want to refresh a ranged dependency.

sections.title: Import the browser entrypoint
paragraphs: Import Chart from chart.js/auto in the hook module. This entrypoint registers Chart.js’s chart types, scales and plugins. JNPM bundles it with the application and Jaspring injects the module after its client runtime.

The import is included in the complete hook below. Keep one top-level chart-hook.ts entrypoint; supporting helpers belong in subdirectories. Remove any older Chart script tag to avoid loading another copy.
sections.code: import Chart from "chart.js/auto";

sections.title: Use the package declarations
paragraphs: Run ./gradlew prepareJnpmTypes and extend the generated JNPM configuration. The compiler and editor can then resolve Chart.js’s public exports and declarations.

Remove the local chart.d.ts used by a previous global-script setup. The hook imports the real Chart class and uses Chart<"bar", number[], string> for numeric bar data. For libraries with separate typings, declare their @types package in api.

sections.title: Wrap it in a hook
paragraphs: Create the widget in mounted and keep it in a WeakMap keyed by the element. Feed new data in updated. Release it in destroyed. Extra methods, such as total here, answer browser calls. The type parameters give el and ctx.params their types, so a wrong field name fails the build.
The canvas carries data-jsp-ignore, so patches keep the attributes and styles that Chart.js sets on it. updated only has to pass the new data.

sections.title: Bind it in a component
paragraphs: Send a record through the json pipe. data-jsp-ignore keeps the canvas as Chart.js left it and lets patches update only its data-* attributes, so new params still reach updated. The stable id lets the morph match the canvas to the same node every time.
The chart sits in its own component, inside a sized wrapper, so the library can measure it and unrelated patches rarely reach it.
sections.code: {{ selected() }}

sections.title: Talk to it from Java
paragraphs: The click arrives as an ordinary event. The total comes back from the hook method through a browser call. Both continuations run in a page turn and write signals.

sections.title: Checklist for any library
paragraphs: Declare browser runtime packages in implementation, use bundled typings or api declarations, and commit jnpm.lock. Node/OS imports such as fs fail bundling, including transitive imports. Keep one widget per element in a WeakMap. Put data-jsp-ignore and a stable id on the element the library owns. Clean up timers, listeners and widget instances in destroyed.

Send data in, not markup. Hook method results may be up to 4 MiB characters over the WebSocket; send files and images to an ordinary endpoint. Libraries that replace or move the hooked element itself do not fit this model; give them a child element they own.
sections.note: The hook uses Chart.js 4.6.1’s npm entrypoint and declarations. Run compileTypescript and lintTypescript after changing the wrapper or package version.

title: Java browser closures
description: Write browser code in Java. Platform.onBrowser runs a lambda in the browser, compiled to WebAssembly at build time.

sections.title: Run a closure
paragraphs: Platform.onBrowser takes a BrowserTask: a lambda that receives a BrowserClient and returns a value. The server sends the lambda's id and captured values to the browser. The compiled body runs there with the real DOM, and the result comes back as JSON.
The ZoneTask completes inside a page turn, so continuations may write signals, exactly like a fork.

sections.title: Wait for a browser promise
paragraphs: Some browser APIs answer later. Use Platform.onBrowserAsync(type, task) when the closure returns a BrowserPromise. The class token names the value type, which erasure hides from the server and the build.
BrowserPromise.then maps the value in the browser before it is sent. There is no way to block on it in Java. BrowserPromise.of(value) wraps a value that is already available.

sections.title: What a closure may do
paragraphs: A closure runs in the browser. It cannot touch Spring beans, signals, services, or this. The build fails and names the method when a lambda uses instance members. Copy what it needs into local variables first.

Captured values and results travel as JSON: primitives and their boxes, String, enums, records of those, and arrays. List, Map<String, T>, and Optional are allowed inside records. At the top level, erasure hides their element type, so wrap them in a record.
Static fields and initialisers of the component class are compiled into the module. Treat that as a hazard, and never capture secrets: everything a closure carries is visible in the page.

sections.title: Work with the host element
paragraphs: client.host() is the component's own host element. Query inside it, read and write attributes, classes, text, and values, move focus, and read bounds.
DOM writes are transient: the next patch morphs the host from server HTML. Lasting state belongs in signals. To report something to the template, dispatch a custom event and bind it as usual.

sections.title: When the build is missing
paragraphs: Without a WebAssembly build, Platform.onBrowser throws BrowserClosuresUnavailableException with the reason. A class recompiled by an IDE or devtools without a new image fails with "stale build" instead of running old code.
In the browser, a call fails with BrowserCallException when the browser lacks WebAssembly GC and exception handling. Current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari 18.2 or later support both.
sections.note: Closures need the Jaspring Gradle plugin and the GraalVM toolchain described in WebAssembly build. Hooks and browser calls do not.

title: BrowserClient API
description: The browser facade a closure receives: the host element, storage, cookies, location, geolocation, clipboard, notifications, and vibration.

sections.title: The facade
paragraphs: Every method of BrowserClient runs in the browser, inside jaspring-browser-runtime. Nothing in it touches the server. The types live in dev.isira.jaspring.browser.

sections.title: Elements
paragraphs: host() returns the component's host element. Element queries are limited to that subtree. bounds() returns getBoundingClientRect() in CSS pixels. value() reads the value property of form controls and is empty for other elements. dispatch sends a bubbling CustomEvent that a template binding receives under $event.detail.
sections.code:
Optional<Element> query(String selector)
List<Element> queryAll(String selector)
Optional<String> attribute(String name)
void attribute(String name, String value)
void removeAttribute(String name)
boolean hasClass(String name)
void addClass(String... names)
void removeClass(String... names)
void toggleClass(String name, boolean on)
String text()            void text(String text)
String value()           void value(String value)
void focus()             void blur()
void scrollIntoView()
ElementBounds bounds()   // x, y, width, height
void dispatch(String type)
void dispatch(String type, String detail)
long viewId()            // HostElement only

sections.title: Storage and cookies
paragraphs: localStorage() and sessionStorage() share the Storage interface. cookies() sees only what JavaScript can see, so HttpOnly cookies are not visible. CookieOptions.DEFAULT uses path /, no max age, not secure, and SameSite Lax.
sections.code:
// Storage
Optional<String> get(String key)
void set(String key, String value)
void remove(String key)
void clear()
List<String> keys()

// Cookies
Optional<String> get(String name)
Map<String, String> all()
void set(String name, String value, CookieOptions options)
void remove(String name)
record CookieOptions(String path, Integer maxAgeSeconds, boolean secure, String sameSite)

sections.title: Location
paragraphs: Location reads window.location. Only the hash may be written. Navigation belongs to the server, through LivePage.redirect.
sections.code:
String href()
String pathname()
String search()
String hash()
void hash(String fragment)

sections.title: Geolocation, clipboard, notifications, vibration
paragraphs: Methods that return BrowserPromise need Platform.onBrowserAsync. The browser asks for permission where the API requires it. The clipboard works only in secure contexts, and reading usually needs a user gesture. Position fields accuracy, altitude, heading, and speed are null when the device does not report them. vibrate returns false when the device cannot vibrate.
sections.code:
// Geolocation
BrowserPromise<Position> current()
BrowserPromise<Position> current(GeolocationOptions options)   // DEFAULT: 10 s timeout
record Position(double latitude, double longitude, Double accuracy, Double altitude,
                Double heading, Double speed, long timestamp)

// Clipboard
BrowserPromise<Void> writeText(String text)
BrowserPromise<String> readText()

// Notifications
PermissionState permission()                 // GRANTED, DENIED, PROMPT
BrowserPromise<PermissionState> requestPermission()
void show(String title, NotificationOptions options)   // no-op without permission

// Vibration
boolean vibrate(int... patternMillis)

sections.title: BrowserPromise
paragraphs: BrowserPromise<T> is a value the browser produces later. then maps it in the browser, before the value is sent to the server. BrowserPromise.of wraps a value that is already available, for closures that only sometimes need to wait.

title: WebAssembly build
description: The Gradle plugin compiles every browser closure into one WebAssembly module with GraalVM Web Image.

sections.title: What you need
paragraphs: Oracle GraalVM 25.2.x, because Web Image is part of Oracle GraalVM and not GraalVM Community. Binaryen's wasm-as 119 or later on the PATH. On Fedora use dnf install binaryen; on macOS use brew install binaryen. Ubuntu 24.04 packages an older version, so use a Binaryen release.
Apply the Jaspring Gradle plugin with the same version as the starter. The plugin adds the matching jaspring-browser-runtime to the jaspringBrowser configuration.

sections.title: The build tasks
paragraphs: The plugin wires three tasks into the build when the java plugin is applied. Projects without closures skip the last two, so applying the plugin costs nothing until you write one. The same plugin also compiles TypeScript; those tasks are covered in TypeScript.
sections.code:
scanBrowserClosures       find BrowserTask lambdas in the compiled classes
compileBrowserDispatcher  compile the generated entry point against jaspring-browser-runtime
buildBrowserImage         native-image --tool:svm-wasm → jaspring-app.js, jaspring-app.js.wasm,
                          jaspring/jaspring-browser.json in the application's resources

sections.title: Configure the build
paragraphs: graalvmHome defaults to GRAALVM_HOME, then to the JDK running Gradle when it is GraalVM. A closure that calls into another library needs that jar on imageClasspath. Library jars are excluded by default, because their Native Image metadata does not apply to the WebAssembly backend.

Without the toolchain the build fails with a message naming what to install. -Pjaspring.browser.skip=true builds without the image. The properties jaspring.browser.graalvmHome and jaspring.browser.assemblerPath are also available.

sections.title: How the module loads
paragraphs: There is one module per application. The server decides per page how to load it. Eager: a component on the page runs a closure while it mounts, so the page preloads the module and the result arrives shortly after first paint. Idle: the application has closures but none run at mount time, so the files are prefetched when the browser is idle, and the runtime starts on the first call or when the user hovers or focuses a handler that runs one. None: no build exists.
Assets are served from /_jaspring/app/<digest>/ with immutable caching. A new build gets new URLs.

sections.title: What it costs
paragraphs: The module size is mostly the Java runtime, so a dozen closures cost about the same as one. Measured on a spike with Oracle GraalVM 25.2.4 and Binaryen 126:
sections.code:
native-image --tool:svm-wasm wall time    25 s
build peak memory                         0.9 GB
module (.js.wasm)                         1.34 MB raw, 487 KB gzip
launcher (.js)                            109 KB
start until the dispatcher is installed   260-290 ms (Node 24)
sections.note: Web Image is experimental in GraalVM 25. Its generated API may change between GraalVM lines, so build with the GraalVM line that matches your Jaspring version.

title: Change detection
description: Understand the page turn: the boundary that keeps Java state, effects, rendering, and browser patches coherent.

sections.title: One page, one turn at a time
paragraphs: A live page owns its component tree, zone, effect scheduler, and page-scoped beans. A turn acquires its lock, binds that context, runs the work, runs change detection, and collects HTML patches.

Initial rendering, browser events, and forked completions are all turns. Turns from one page never overlap. Different pages can execute concurrently on virtual threads. Rendering sibling subtrees within a page is sequential.

sections.title: Default and OnPush
paragraphs: In zone mode, every turn ends in a tick. Default views re-render. OnPush views update when an input changes, an event fires inside the view, a signal read by it changes, or markForCheck is called.

sections.title: Choose zoneless mode
paragraphs: In zoneless mode, only dirty views re-render. Signal reads connect each template to its dependencies, and writes mark those views dirty. Use ChangeDetectorRef.current() inside a constructor or hook for markForCheck, detectChanges, detach, and reattach.
sections.code:
jaspring:
  change-detection: zoneless
  stability-timeout: 300ms

sections.title: From effects to patches
paragraphs: Effects run before views during each tick. A tick repeats while effects or renders dirty more state, with a limit of ten passes. Jaspring does not implement Angular’s development-only expression-changed second pass.

The server caches each component’s rendered HTML. After a turn, the topmost changed views become patches. The browser morphs those HTML fragments into the live document rather than replacing the entire page.

title: Gradle & IDE tooling
description: Generate components with a familiar command, and keep Java-backed templates comfortable to work in.

sections.title: Apply the Gradle plugin
paragraphs: The Jaspring plugin provides build tooling: component scaffolding, the TypeScript build of browser scripts, and the WebAssembly build of Java browser closures. Keep the starter dependency for the runtime. Add Maven Central to plugin repositories, then apply the same version as the starter.
Jaspring 0.5.0 includes JNPM for npm dependencies, browser bundles and ESLint. The JNPM guide covers dependency scopes, lockfiles and package imports.

sections.title: Generate a component
paragraphs: The task creates a Java class and package-relative HTML and CSS resources. It refuses to overwrite existing targets. By default, each component gets its own subpackage; --flat omits that final directory.
sections.code:
./gradlew generateComponent --name=user-card --package=com.example.components

# Generated files:
# src/main/java/com/example/components/usercard/UserCardComponent.java
# src/main/resources/com/example/components/usercard/user-card.component.html
# src/main/resources/com/example/components/usercard/user-card.component.css

sections.title: Shape the output
paragraphs: Options include --prefix, --selector, --inline-template, --inline-style, --display-block, --style=none, and --change-detection=OnPush. Parent paths in a name become Java subpackages. Use a qualified task such as :app:generateComponent in a multi-module application.
The task creates component files only. It does not generate routes, controllers, tests, TypeScript, Sass, or NgModules. List the available options with ./gradlew help --task generateComponent.
sections.code: ./gradlew generateComponent --name=counter              --package=com.example.components --flat              --inline-template --inline-style --change-detection=OnPush

sections.title: Compile TypeScript
paragraphs: With the java plugin applied, the plugin adds two tasks that run before processResources. extractTypescriptTypes writes jaspring.d.ts and tsconfig.base.json to build/jaspring/typescript/types/ for the editor. compileTypescript type-checks src/main/typescript and ships the compiled jaspring/ts/**/*.js files and the jaspring/jaspring-typescript.json manifest with the application's resources. Projects without src/main/typescript skip both.

The compiler is dev.isira:jaspring-typescript on the jaspringTypescript configuration. The plugin adds its own version by default. The typescript block is optional; these are the defaults. Each setting also has a Gradle property: jaspring.typescript.typeCheck, jaspring.typescript.host, jaspring.typescript.nodePath, and jaspring.typescript.skip.
sections.note: The TypeScript page covers the compiler hosts, the editor setup, and the startup fallback.

sections.title: Install and bundle browser packages
paragraphs: With JNPM, a top-level jnpm block declares implementation, api, devImplementation and devApi packages. Run jnpmLock, commit jnpm.lock, then build normally. Packages and generated npm files live under build/.

compileTypescript installs the lock and prepares declarations before checking and bundling the browser entrypoints. check runs ESLint. Node/OS API imports fail bundling, and packages are never installed at application startup.
sections.code:
jnpmLock           create or reconcile the dependency lock
jnpmUpdate         refresh versions within declared ranges
jnpmInstall        install the exact lock
prepareJnpmTypes   prepare types and editor metadata
compileTypescript  check and bundle
lintTypescript     report lint diagnostics
fixTypescript      apply fixes explicitly
sections.note: This guide requires the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin and matching starter. Follow Installation for the Maven Central setup.

sections.title: IntelliJ IDEA support
paragraphs: The framework repository includes a standalone IntelliJ plugin under tools/intellij-plugin. It supplies Java-backed template completion, navigation, and refactoring support. Follow that directory’s README for its build and installation instructions.

The IntelliJ plugin’s JNPM integration imports dependency scopes through the Gradle model and prepares dependencies after sync. With JavaScript/TypeScript support installed, it provides ESLint diagnostics and fixes for unsaved text. Template features remain available without either optional integration.

Tools → JNPM offers dependency preparation, lock reconciliation and updates. Application run configurations receive a compileTypescript before-run task. A missing lock requires explicit reconciliation; sync never writes it. Supported IDE lines are IntelliJ IDEA 2026.2 and 2026.3.

title: Under the hood
description: Three familiar foundations, one live application model. Follow a page from compilation to a browser patch.

sections.title: A meta-framework, by composition
paragraphs: Spring Boot provides the application, MVC integration, dependency injection, and transports. Angular’s compiler supplies template parsing. GraalJS runs the compiler and PostCSS at startup. Jaspring implements the Java component model, expression evaluation, signals, page turns, and HTML patching.

This gives you Angular’s template language without running a conventional Angular application in the browser. The browser receives rendered HTML and a small client runtime. Java browser closures optionally add a WebAssembly application module.

sections.title: At startup
paragraphs: Classpath scanning discovers Jaspring components, pipes, and directives. Angular’s real compiler parses each template in GraalJS. Jaspring converts the result into Java AST records, resolves members, and validates the template.
PostCSS scopes component CSS; Tailwind runs here too if configured. Invalid templates fail startup with Angular’s compiler messages. The server does not evaluate JavaScript on the request path.

sections.title: At render and event time
paragraphs: A controller returns JaspringView. The runtime creates a live page and renders its component tree in a turn. It waits for tracked work up to the configured stability timeout and wraps the result in the HTML layout.

The browser sends bound events back to that page. Java runs the handler under the page lock, change detection chooses changed views, and the transport delivers HTML patches. The browser runtime morphs the corresponding DOM.
sections.code:
Browser event
    → page turn + Java handler
    → signal writes + change detection
    → changed component HTML
    → WebSocket or HTTP
    → browser DOM patch

sections.title: The framework modules
paragraphs: jaspring-core owns the component, template, signal, zone, and live-page machinery. jaspring-spring-boot-starter adds auto-configuration, MVC views, layouts, live transports, browser assets, and serving of compiled TypeScript.

jaspring-gradle-plugin provides component scaffolding, the TypeScript build, and browser-closure builds. jaspring-typescript is the TypeScript 6 compiler hosted in GraalJS or Node, used by the plugin and by the starter's startup fallback. jaspring-browser-runtime is the BrowserClient facade compiled into WebAssembly. jaspring-sample shows the pieces working together.

The JNPM pipeline belongs to jaspring-gradle-plugin. Java coordinates the build, npm resolves and installs the locked graph, esbuild emits browser assets, and ESLint checks the sources. Those build tools do not run inside packaged applications.

title: Configuration
description: A small set of application-level choices for rendering, transports, page lifetime, and styling.

sections.title: Configure the runtime
paragraphs: Jaspring uses Spring Boot configuration properties under jaspring. Enable virtual threads for the application. Use dev-mode during development when you want detailed handler errors returned to the browser.
sections.code:
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true

jaspring:
  change-detection: zone
  live:
    transport: websocket
  stability-timeout: 10s
  page-ttl: 60s
  max-pages-per-session: 20
  dev-mode: false

sections.title: Page lifetime and stability
paragraphs: stability-timeout controls how long the initial render waits for Zone-managed work. Later completions arrive as patches. It defaults to ten seconds. A lower timeout can expose a loading state sooner.

page-ttl is how long a page survives without a connected client, defaulting to sixty seconds. max-pages-per-session defaults to twenty. Each live page owns server-side state, so choose deployment capacity with that lifetime in mind.

sections.title: Layout and component discovery
paragraphs: The default layout is classpath:/jaspring/index.html. Add that resource to customize the document head, fonts, global CSS, and scripts. Include an empty root-selector element; Jaspring replaces it with rendered component HTML.
Component discovery defaults to the @SpringBootApplication packages. Set jaspring.base-packages when components live elsewhere.
sections.code:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>My Jaspring app</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/site.css">
</head>
<body><app-root></app-root></body>
</html>

sections.title: TypeScript at startup
paragraphs: For applications without JNPM, adding dev.isira:jaspring-typescript to the runtime classpath lets the starter compile stale or missing source builds at startup, such as an IDE launch that bypassed Gradle. These are the defaults. A packaged application has no sources, so the build manifest stands.
sections.code:
jaspring:
  typescript:
    enabled: true
    type-check: true
    source-dir: src/main/typescript
    host: graaljs
sections.note: JNPM applications build before launch. With the development compiler present, a missing or stale bundle fails startup with an instruction to run compileTypescript. The source-only fallback never installs npm packages.

sections.title: Opt into Tailwind
paragraphs: Set jaspring.tailwind.stylesheet to a classpath CSS resource to enable Tailwind’s startup compilation. Without this property, ordinary global and component styles work without Tailwind.
sections.code:
jaspring:
  tailwind:
    stylesheet: classpath:tailwind.css

title: Status & compatibility
description: Familiar syntax comes with a different execution model. Know the current boundaries before building on them.

sections.title: Experimental, and usable for exploration
paragraphs: The Jaspring 0.5.0 starter implements server-rendered components, live browser events, signals, zone and zoneless change detection, client hooks, browser calls, Java-to-WebAssembly browser closures, and browser scripts in TypeScript. Static generation and incremental regeneration remain future work.

A live page keeps its component tree and state on the server between events. Interaction depends on a working connection. Evaluate that architecture and the experimental API against your application’s needs.

JNPM is included in Jaspring 0.5.0. Its Gradle dependency scopes, browser bundling and ESLint are available through the release plugin. The separate IntelliJ plugin adds dependency import, diagnostics and before-run builds.

sections.title: Maven build limitations
paragraphs: Maven can use the Jaspring Spring Boot starter for server-rendered components, templates, signals, styling and live events. The runtime dependency does not apply the Gradle plugin, and there is no Jaspring Maven build plugin.

Maven has no integrated compileTypescript task for build-time type checking and packaging browser scripts. It also cannot run JNPM’s dependency installation, lockfile management, browser bundling or ESLint tasks. Use Gradle for this workflow; prebuilt assets or a custom build integration must otherwise be supplied separately.

Component generation and compilation of Platform.onBrowser Java closures to WebAssembly are also Gradle plugin tasks. Maven does not provide them, and the IntelliJ plugin’s JNPM dependency import and before-run build require a Gradle project.

Package-free TypeScript can still use the startup fallback: add the matching dev.isira:jaspring-typescript dependency with runtime scope and make the sources available in src/main/typescript or classpath:/typescript/. It compiles and serves scripts from memory at startup. It does not add a Maven compilation step, install npm packages or enable JNPM.
sections.note: JNPM is included in the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin. Adding the 0.5.0 starter to a Maven build does not enable its build tooling.

sections.title: Angular syntax, Java behavior
paragraphs: Templates are parsed by Angular’s compiler, but execution happens against Java objects. Signal and input equality use Objects.equals. Numeric results are Long or Double, then coerced at typed Java boundaries.

All scanned components, pipes, and directives are currently globally visible. Angular standalone import boundaries are not enforced. References on ordinary elements contain server-side element metadata, not browser DOM nodes.

sections.title: Rendering and lifecycle boundaries
paragraphs: @defer renders placeholders unless hydrate triggers call for the main content. Server triggers do not run. ICU plural categories currently cover English categories. Dates and numbers use JDK locale data rather than Angular’s CLDR data.

Effects run before views in page ticks. Sibling lifecycle phases are not batched exactly like Angular. There is no development-mode ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked second pass and no parallel sibling rendering.

sections.title: Browser and trust boundaries
paragraphs: Event preventDefault and stopPropagation flags are decided when handlers render. The HTML sanitizer uses an Angular-derived allowlist over a tolerant tokenizer instead of a browser DOM parser.

Java browser closures run client-side. Captures and results cross the network as JSON; never capture secrets. The optional WebAssembly runtime needs a compatible browser and Oracle GraalVM’s build tooling.

JNPM application packages must work in the browser. Node/OS imports such as fs and child_process, including transitive imports, fail the build. Native Node addons and dependency lifecycle scripts are unsupported. Build-time development tools run separately in managed Node.
Report reproducible issues in the framework’s GitHub repository. Include the smallest component, template, configuration, and steps that demonstrate the behavior.
sections.note: Keep the Gradle plugin, starter, and core on the same version. The plugin adds the matching jaspring-browser-runtime and jaspring-typescript to its builds.

title: Font Awesome icons
description: Install Font Awesome through JNPM and bundle its CSS and web fonts. Icons remain ordinary template elements through live patches.

sections.title: Why it just works
paragraphs: Font Awesome's web font version is plain CSS and font files. Icons are ordinary <i> elements in server HTML, so they render on first paint and survive every patch.

JNPM bundles imported stylesheets and the font files they reference. Jaspring links the generated CSS once in the page head and serves the fonts from the application’s own /_jaspring/ts/ assets. Icon rendering uses CSS and web fonts; no client hook or icon-replacement script is needed.
sections.note: This guide requires the Jaspring 0.5.0 Gradle plugin and matching starter. Follow Installation for the Maven Central setup.

sections.title: Declare the npm package
paragraphs: Add the scoped @fortawesome/fontawesome-free package to jnpm. Use implementation because its CSS and font files are browser assets. This CSS-only usage needs no api declaration package.
Run ./gradlew jnpmLock and commit jnpm.lock alongside the Gradle declaration. Then run ./gradlew build to install the exact lock, check the TypeScript entrypoint and emit the assets.

sections.title: Import the stylesheet
paragraphs: Create a top-level TypeScript entrypoint and import the package stylesheet. JNPM follows its relative font URLs, emits hashed CSS and font files, and rewrites the references to those emitted assets.

Jaspring adds the generated stylesheet and entry module to live pages automatically. Import the CSS once, either in icons.ts or in an existing entrypoint. When migrating, remove the old Font Awesome stylesheet link and its WebJar dependency to avoid duplicate styles and fonts.
sections.code: import "@fortawesome/fontawesome-free/css/all.min.css";
sections.note: Use the tsconfig.jnpm.json editor setup from JNPM. Its generated declarations cover CSS imports. Keep jaspring.live.transport enabled: automatic bundle styles and scripts are injected together with the client runtime.

sections.title: Use icons in templates
paragraphs: Write icons as usual. Bindings work on them like any element, so an icon can follow a signal. Mark decorative icons with aria-hidden and give icon-only buttons a label.
sections.code:
@for (item of items(); track item.id) {
  • {{ item.name }}
    • }

sections.title: Styles and Tailwind
paragraphs: Font Awesome's CSS is global, so emulated encapsulation does not scope it and icons work in every component. Size and color icons from component styles or with Tailwind utilities on the <i> element. Tailwind sees fa-* names as candidates and ignores them, so the two do not conflict.

sections.title: Keep icons as web fonts
paragraphs: Font Awesome also ships an SVG + JavaScript version that replaces <i> tags with <svg> in the browser. Avoid it with Jaspring. Each patch morphs the view back to the server HTML, which has the <i>, and the script then replaces it again. You get extra DOM work and flicker on every update.
If you need inline SVG, render the SVG markup from the server in a small icon component instead.

sections.title: Updates and offline builds
paragraphs: To upgrade this exact version, change the JNPM declaration, run jnpmLock and review the lockfile diff. If you choose a semver range instead, jnpmUpdate refreshes versions within it. Normal builds keep the committed resolutions.

The application JAR contains the emitted CSS, fonts and license notices. Deployment does not need npm or node_modules. clean removes the build installation; after an online build has cached the packages, an offline build reinstalls them from Gradle’s user cache.
sections.code:
./gradlew jnpmLock
./gradlew build

# Once the toolchain and packages are cached:
./gradlew clean build --offline
